summaries.example: Imagine two toy blocks that look alike. They are the same color, size, shape, and weight. Are they still two blocks? The Identity of Indiscernibles asks whether two things could be different objects while matching in every important way. Some philosophers say no: if there really are two blocks, there must be some difference between them. Others say it might be possible for two objects to match perfectly.
summaries.summary: The Identity of Indiscernibles is a philosophical idea about when two things can count as different. It says that there cannot be two objects that differ only because they are two objects; they must also differ in how they are. Philosophers debate what “how they are” includes. It might mean all properties, only pure properties that do not name a particular object, or only intrinsic pure properties that do not depend on outside things. A very weak version can become true just because objects have different identity labels, so philosophers try to avoid such easy answers. Max Black’s example of two matching iron spheres challenges stronger versions. Other philosophers have offered arguments for the principle, including arguments about reasons, properties, and the nature of objects. The entry explains that the debate is not settled and that different versions have different consequences.
key_ideas: The main idea says that two different objects must differ in more than simply being two objects.
Philosophers disagree about which properties should count. Properties such as “being this exact object” may make the claim too easy.
Some versions look at pure properties, which do not refer to a particular named thing. Other versions look only at intrinsic properties, which do not depend on outside relationships.
Max Black imagined a world containing two matching iron spheres. This thought experiment is a famous challenge to the principle.
The principle has connections to objects in mathematics, physical particles, properties, and possible worlds.
summaries.why_it_matters: This question helps us think carefully about what makes one thing different from another. It also connects to questions about whether space, time, particles, mathematical objects, and properties can have perfect matches. Studying it teaches an important philosophical habit: before arguing about a principle, clarify exactly what its words mean.

important_terms.definition: Being one object rather than two or more objects. Two blocks have numerical difference if there are really two blocks.
A difference in how things are, such as a difference in color, size, or shape.
A feature that something has, such as being red, round, warm, or next to another object.
Unable to be told apart by the chosen features or relationships being considered.

questions_to_think_about: If two things matched in every way we could observe, would they still be two things?
Should a property such as “being this exact block” count as a real difference for this question?
Could two objects have the same inside features but different places?
Does imagining a situation prove that it could really be possible?

summaries.example: Consider a possible world containing only two iron spheres. They have the same size, color, temperature, shape, and every other pure property, but they occupy different locations. Are there two spheres, or could the description amount to one object with two locations? Max Black used a case of this kind to challenge strong forms of the Identity of Indiscernibles. Replies differ: some say the spheres are related to one another and therefore weakly discernible; others argue that this does not provide the required difference in pure properties. The dispute shows why both the property vocabulary and the interpretation of possibility matter.
summaries.summary: The Identity of Indiscernibles claims that distinct objects cannot differ merely numerically: any two objects must differ in some further respect. The claim is not a single fixed principle because its modal force, domain, and relevant kind of difference can vary. Contemporary discussion usually treats extra-numerical difference as difference in properties. Yet unrestricted properties make the claim trivial, since properties such as being identical with a particular object can distinguish objects without describing how they are. The entry therefore focuses on non-trivializing properties, pure properties, and intrinsic pure properties. These generate a weaker-to-stronger ordering of versions. Quine’s forms instead classify discernibility by the kinds of predicates or relations involved, although weak discernibility can become trivial if numerical difference itself is allowed to do the work. Arguments against the principle include Black’s two-sphere scenario, recombination arguments, and cases involving physical duplicates. Arguments for it draw on Leibnizian explanations, sufficient reason, bundle theories, and views about the autonomy of objects, but each depends on controversial assumptions. The principle also bears on anti-haecceitism, mathematical and physical objects, and the grounds of identity, without being identical to any of those theories.
key_ideas: The principle has several versions. The weakest main version concerns all non-trivializing properties; stronger versions concern all pure properties or all intrinsic pure properties.
The hierarchy matters: the intrinsic-pure version entails the pure-property version, which entails the non-trivializing-property version.
Quine-inspired versions distinguish absolute, relative, and weak discernibility. Weak discernibility involves a relation that two objects bear to each other but not to themselves.
The strongest versions face proposed counterexamples involving matching leaves, water drops, manufactured objects, physical particles, and Black’s two-sphere world.

Arguments for the principle appeal to Leibniz’s complete concepts, sufficient reason, bundle theories, and claims about the independence of objects. The entry also explains objections to these arguments.

The principle is a supervenience thesis: once the relevant properties are fixed, facts about numerical identity are fixed. It is not automatically a theory of what grounds identity, nor does it by itself establish anti-haecceitism.
summaries.why_it_matters: The issue tests a central metaphysical question: is an object fully determined by its qualitative features, or can there be primitive differences between otherwise matching objects? It also clarifies distinctions that recur throughout philosophy, including property types, necessity, possible worlds, supervenience, and grounding. Because small changes in the formulation produce importantly different claims, the debate is a useful lesson in precision and argument analysis.

important_terms.definition: The thesis that necessarily, no two objects are alike with respect to all properties of the relevant kind; numerical difference requires some further difference.
A difference concerning which objects things are, rather than a difference in their features or ways of being.
A difference in how objects are, usually explained by their differing in at least one relevant property.
A feature or characteristic instantiated by an object, such as being red or having a particular relation.
A property that does not refer to any particular named object, such as being red or being next to a tower.
Roughly, a property whose possession does not depend on how its bearer is related to things outside it.
A property whose difference between objects is not merely a difference in which objects they are; pure properties are included, but some impure properties may be included too.
A relation in which one fact depends on another for its existence or explanation. The entry distinguishes this from the Identity of Indiscernibles, which is primarily a supervenience claim.

questions_to_think_about: Which properties should be excluded as trivializing, and can that boundary be drawn without assuming the conclusion?
Does a relation between two objects make them genuinely discernible, or only weakly discernible?
Does the possibility of imagining two perfect duplicates show that such objects are metaphysically possible?
Could a bundle theory remain true if two objects had exactly the same constituents?
Why might a principle about objects within one possible world fail to settle questions about objects across different possible worlds?

summaries.example: Suppose a factory makes two brand-new, identical-looking water bottles. They have the same shape, color, size, temperature, and contents. You can still point to one as “this bottle” and the other as “that bottle.” The philosophical question is whether that pointing gives a real difference in how the bottles are, or merely shows that there are two objects. Some philosophers think there must be another difference, even if we cannot find it. Others think two perfectly matching objects might be possible.
summaries.summary: The Identity of Indiscernibles is the claim that different objects must differ in more than simply being different objects. Philosophers usually explain this by saying that they must differ in some relevant property. But the exact version of the principle depends on which properties are allowed. If identity properties are included, any two objects can be distinguished by properties such as “being identical with the first object,” making the claim trivial. The entry therefore discusses non-trivializing properties, pure properties that do not refer to particular things, and intrinsic properties that do not depend on outside relations. The resulting versions vary in strength. A famous challenge, associated with Max Black, imagines two matching iron spheres in an otherwise empty world. The entry surveys reasons to accept and reject such examples, including questions about physical particles, possible worlds, and whether imagination establishes possibility. It also connects the principle with bundle theories, anti-haecceitism, and theories about what explains identity. The overall lesson is that the principle cannot be evaluated fairly until its terms and scope are carefully specified.
key_ideas: Philosophers must decide what counts as a relevant difference. Including identity properties can make the principle true in an uninteresting way.
There are three important versions: one uses non-trivializing properties, one uses pure properties, and one uses intrinsic pure properties.
The intrinsic-pure version is strongest. If it is true, the other two versions follow; the reverse does not necessarily follow.
Max Black’s thought experiment imagines two iron spheres with matching properties. If that situation is possible, it challenges strong versions of the principle.
Supporters use ideas about sufficient reasons, complete descriptions of individual substances, and objects being bundles of properties. Critics question the assumptions behind these arguments.

The principle is related to, but different from, anti-haecceitism. The principle concerns whether different objects can match; anti-haecceitism concerns whether different possibilities can match qualitatively.
summaries.why_it_matters: The question affects how we understand individuality. If every object is fixed by its properties, then there may be no room for objects that are perfect qualitative duplicates. If duplicates are possible, then being a particular object may not be fully explained by its qualities. The debate also shows how metaphysical arguments depend on careful choices about properties, possibility, and explanation.

important_terms.definition: The idea that two different things cannot match in every relevant way. If they are really two objects, they must differ somehow besides just being two.
The fact that two things are not one and the same object.
A difference in an object’s features or way of being, rather than merely its identity as a separate object.
A feature an object has, such as being blue, heavy, round, or next to another object.
A property that does not mention a particular individual, such as being blue or being next to a tower.
A property that, roughly, does not depend on relationships with things outside the object.
A property that helps show how an object is different, rather than merely identifying it by name or reference.

questions_to_think_about: Can two objects be exactly alike without being the same object?
Should location count as a property that distinguishes objects?
Why is “being this particular object” often considered an unfair answer?
Does a thought experiment show what is possible, or only what we can imagine?
What kinds of evidence would make a proposed counterexample convincing?
